title: Six Takeaways from "Sold a Story"
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Pondiscio reacts to Emily Hanford's new Sold a Story episodes on Steubenville, Ohio, where a 25-year commitment to Success for All has produced strong reading results. He draws six lessons: continuity matters more than chasing trends, SFA is well evidenced, scripted curricula such as SFA and Direct Instruction suffer from teacher distaste for scripts, teacher buy-in is essential, and EdReports and state approved lists are mixed blessings. His case is that standards alignment is not a measure of quality and that lists built on flawed tools nearly excluded a proven program. He ties the buy-in point to his own observation of school culture at Success Academy. He closes that education has too much innovation and too little execution.
points: Steubenville's results are attributed to continuity: minimal churn in curriculum, staff and leadership over a quarter-century.
Scripted programs such as SFA and DI are held back less by evidence than by teachers' preference for freedom over recipes.
Teacher buy-in, including SFA's adoption vote, is decisive: even the best program flops without it.
EdReports was built for Common Core alignment, which is neutral on text quality and nearly sidelined SFA in Ohio.
State approved-curriculum lists help only if they rest on evidence rather than flawed review tools.
quotes: In education, especially for schools serving disadvantaged kids, curriculum changes as often as losing baseball teams swap managers—new year, new playbook, same old slump. Not so in Steubenville, where sticking with SFA for 25 years has been a game-changer.

Minimal churn—low teacher turnover, a decade-long superintendent, and 48% of staff are local grads—breeds a stability other schools and districts can only envy. Hanford gets baffled looks when she asks Steubenville teachers if they’d ever heard of Lucy Calkins, Fountas and Pinnell, or even balanced literacy.

Teachers tend to valorize freedom over recipes, and that resistance keeps SFA and DI niche, even with Steubenville’s success and DI’s decades of data. Could “Sold a Story” change that misperception? We’ll see.

In How the Other Half Learns, I expected to write about curriculum and instruction at Success Academy but surprised myself by writing more about school culture: The X factor that makes those schools soar is every adult in a kid’s life singing from the same hymnal. SFA gets that: Without teachers on board, even the best program flops.

But Hanford’s reporting echoes a worry I’ve harbored: Standards alignment isn’t enough. Built for Common Core, EdReports encourages a view of reading that is neutral-to-agnostic on quality. A “standards-based” view of reading means you can teach Dickens or dreck.

Education’s cursed with too much innovation, not enough execution. These episodes scream it louder. Hanford’s work remains a wake-up call, and these episodes raise the stakes: We’ve got the evidence, so why aren’t we using it?
